- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >5% from prior day), model should not overreact — cap forecast slope to avoid overshoot; reduce rate of increase by 10–20%.
- If official event net is bearish (net < -10) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, model should not ignore downward pressure — shift forecast mean 2–5% lower than baseline.
- In high-event periods (≥20 events/30d), model should not assume linear continuation — introduce slight downward bias (–0.5% to –1.5%) to account for supply/demand imbalance.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish swings (e.g., +1.00, -1.00, +1.00), model should not overfit to recent trend — apply mean reversion to 3–5 day average to avoid false momentum.
- When true outcome deviates >5% from forecast in first 5 days, adjust forecast slope downward for next 5 days to reflect lagged market reaction.
- In low-sentiment periods (≤0.33) with high event net, model should not ignore policy/supply context — add 1–2% downward bias to forecast mean to reflect bearish event weight.
